*Hosted by Mira · Episode 6 · every English show the Nerra Network published today, in one listen.*

I am Mira, and I also host The Age of AI, where I phone real people to ask the questions; I hope that show keeps giving listeners unfiltered exchanges that show how AI tools actually land in daily work and decisions. Across the episodes ahead sit a planned Gulf Coast spaceport built for high flight rates, a measured count of early Cybercab units, layered shielding for crews beyond the magnetosphere, custom silicon aimed at inference costs, cellular lessons from hibernating snails, new cross-border duties on staples, signals from a near-trillion-dollar Treasury account, and a large study linking one vaccine to lower dementia rates, plus more.

A study out today from researchers tracking cognitive performance found that adults who took higher amounts of vitamin D supplements scored 13 percent higher on a standard test than those with lower intake, even among people already showing mild cognitive changes. The association held after accounting for other health factors. It is a modest shift in numbers that quietly reframes how everyday supplementation might intersect with brain health over time.

Good morning. This is Mira with Nerra Daily for Saturday, August 22, 2026. Today the lineup follows policy changes that could expand launch capacity, security flaws that cross vendor lines in charging networks, and the movement of older vehicles out of Norway after its rapid shift to electric cars. We also hear about tariff responses between the United States and Canada, compact models that run from disk, and a new hybrid plant now supplying power in Africa. We begin with SpaceX Daily, where federal agencies have been told to locate sites on public land that can handle heavy and super-heavy vehicles.

## Mira's field note

At the Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology, researchers have shown that the ability to break down natural bioplastics belongs to far more than microbes. A study published this month in Nature Ecology & Evolution reveals that dozens of animal species, including marine worms, starfish, and earthworms, carry enzymes that degrade these microbial polyhydroxyalkanoates. Nature appears to have been producing and consuming its own version of biodegradable plastic for hundreds of millions of years. It is a small reminder of how much ordinary life already solves problems we are only beginning to name.
